<reason>B better establishes why targeted expansion restrictions justify some forgone earnings: destructive conversion imposes potentially irreversible costs on other livelihoods. A raises serious enforcement and leakage objections, but B answers with focused permitting, retained existing production, and benefits that partial displacement does not automatically erase. A’s mapped-enforcement alternative concedes usable capacity, weakening its categorical implementation objection. Its later treatment of uncertain leakage as proof that benefits remain wholly unproven overstates B’s concession. B provides the clearer marginal-policy comparison and more directly resolves the central tradeoff.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s closing effectively challenges A’s “certain costs, speculative benefits” asymmetry: when a damaging conversion is prevented, lost expansion earnings and protected land follow from the same decision. B also explains how closing exceptions can use the existing mapped boundaries that A’s alternative already relies upon.</best_rebuttal>
